ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY 
Functional materials - Polymers

Organic Light Emitting Diodes (OLEDs)
Work in a similar way to conventional diodes and LEDs, but instead of using layers of n-type and p-type semiconductors, they use organic molecules
OLEDs have an emissive electroluminescent layer which is a film of organic compound that emits light in response to an electric current
Also known as  organic EL (electroluminescent) diodes
Solid-state devices made of thin films of organic molecules that emit light on application of electricity

Offer high contrast, brighter displays with wider viewing angle

Bulk

Molecules

Emissive layer: 
These organic materials have electrical conductivity in the range of semiconductors.

The concept of highest occupied and lowest unoccupied molecular orbitals (HOMO and LUMO) in molecules is analogous to the valence and conduction bands in bulk materials.

We can choose the materials according to the band gap

Blue-emitting materials have a larger band gap

Source slide page 10 (extracted text):
ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY 
Functional materials - Polymers

Why Multi-Layered Structure?
Inorganic semiconductors have a higher conductivity than the organic materials, so a layered structure is not needed.

Organic materials have a lower conductivity than the inorganic counterparts

HOMOs and LUMOs of the materials in the layered structure act as small steps and guide the charge carriers to the emissive layer.
The layered structure helps maintain a smoother carrier flow.

Transcript block 1 (source interval 000000-000299 seconds):
[00:00:00.612] Hello everyone, welcome back to this course on engineering chemistry.
[00:00:06.628] We will study module 7a today about organic light emitting diodes. This is the only class in this topic, and we are going to study about the construction, working, the types of OLEDs, the advantages, disadvantages, and applications.
[00:00:26.692] First, let us understand the working of light emitting diodes, because the same concept can be extended to organic light emitting diodes.
[00:00:37.380] So an LED as it is popularly known has an N type and a P type semiconductor which is forming a PN junction. The most common material is gallium arsenide, which is used to make these LEDs.
[00:00:56.324] Further doping is done and we have different types of colored LEDs. Now when voltage is applied across the junction, the electrons and the holes they move towards each other as you can see in the picture here.
[00:01:13.312] And they recombine in the depletion layer. When they recombine, they give out a photon and that is what we see as light. So that is the how an LED works. Now let us understand what is an O LED.
[00:01:31.364] So as the name suggests, we are going to use some organic molecules. So they work in a similar way to the conventional diodes and the LEDs, but instead of using layers N type and P type of semiconductors,
[00:01:47.312] They use organic molecules and hence the name organic light emitting diodes. The phenomena which is happening in OLEDs is called electroluminescence. Therefore, OLEDs
[00:02:03.172] have an emissive electroluminescent layer, which is a film of an organic compound that emits light in response to an electric current. Hence they are also known as organic electroluminescent diodes.
[00:02:20.292] So let us have a clear definition of what is an OLED. So we can define them as solid state devices which are made up of thin films of organic molecules that emit light on application of electricity.
[00:02:40.708] The first OLED device was made by Eastman Kodak in the nineteen eighties. So we know Kodak Labs, it was first made there and it's an emerging technology for displays. All of us have seen
[00:02:57.764] OLED TVs, so much advertisement for OLED mobile displays. So why are they so important? Because these displays can be flexible, they can be very thin and of light weight.
[00:03:13.924] Moreover, the power consumption is less as compared to the conventional LEDs and the L C Ds. Apart from that, they offer a high contrast, brighter displays with wider viewing angle.
[00:03:29.796] So being flexible is a very big advantage which OLEDs give us. So you can see in the picture here how nicely the display is foldable. And here you can actually roll it. So these kind of advantages make O L E Ds
[00:03:47.536] a topic of research and it is an emerging technology for displays. Let us understand the construction.
[00:03:58.756] So we have a layered structure as you can see in the picture here. First of all, there is a substrate which is made of glass and that is basically for support. On the substrate, we can see the anode. This is usually transparent and made of
[00:04:16.804] indium tin oxide it is ITO and then we have two organic layers here as you can see this orange layer over here is known as the conductive layer and it is going to transport holes from the
[00:04:34.468] anode and this is usually made of polyaniline and also there are other kind of material organic molecules which are used to make this conductive layer.
[00:04:48.580] And then we also have the next layer which is again an organic uh mole made of organic molecules and this is known as the emissive layer.
[00:04:59.012] And here we have these this is very very important because this is where the light emission happens. So it helps in transporting electrons from the cathode and a recombination of electrons and poles takes place here.

Transcript block 2 (source interval 000300-000599 seconds):
[00:05:15.776] and light is emitted. One example of a polymer which is used. So we should understand that it could be organic molecules or polymers which can make up these conductive layer, this conductive layer and the emissive layer. So in emissive layer we use polyflorine
[00:05:34.276] And the cathode of course is used to inject electrons and it is usually made with metals like magnesium which have a low work function. Now let us understand the working of an OLED.
[00:05:51.268] A voltage is applied across the anode and cathode of the OLED. So let us look at this picture very carefully here. We can see that the cathode will be connected to the negative terminal, hence there are
[00:06:06.960] Electrons coming from the cathode. So these electrons now move into the emissive layer. The green layer you can see here, these are moving to the emissive layers from emissive layer from the cathode. And at the same time, electrons.
[00:06:23.728] uh which have moved out of this
[00:06:27.556] orange layer over here which is the conductive layer. So therefore what happens? Holes have now moved into the conductive layer. So holes are getting transported from the anode into the conductive layer and electrons are getting transported from the cathode into the emissive layer.
[00:06:44.740] Now these electrons and holes they will combine and thereby emit and emit a photon. Now this recombination happens closer to the emissive layer. You can see here closer to the emissive layer and therefore
[00:07:02.208] light is being emitted from the emissive layer. Now the color of the light is going to depend on the organic molecule which is being used.
[00:07:15.716] And the intensity of the light, that is the brightness of the light, is going to depend on the current density.
[00:07:24.228] So we can understand that there are electrons which are moving from the cathode into the emissive layer, and there are holes which are moving to the conductive layer from the anode. These two are going the holes in the electrons are going to
[00:07:40.688] combine and this combination happens closer to the emissive layer and that is how whenever there's a combination of a electron and a hole then there will be emission of light. So basically what is happening the combination of electron and hole what we understand. Now the electrons are at
[00:07:58.320] And the holes are at a lower energy level. So we can say the electrons are in the lowest unoccupied molecule molecular orbitals and the holes are now in the
[00:08:11.312] uh Homo that is highest occupied molecular orbital. So when these electrons come back from a higher energy level to the lower energy level, we know that a photon is given out or energy is given out and that is the radiation. We have learned this in right from
[00:08:28.976] spectros molecular spectroscopy when we were studying. Whenever there is an electron transition from a higher level to the lower level, the energy is uh given out in the form of a radiation, and here it is in the visible uh region. So we are seeing the
[00:08:43.728] uh light. So this color of this light obviously will depend on the energy gap and of course that is going to depend on the organic molecules which we are using and the intensity of course will depend on the current density.
[00:08:59.556] Now let us study different types of O LEDs which are available.
[00:09:05.796] We have passive matrix OLED, which is known as the emolet, and we have the active matrix matrix OLED, that is the emolet. Then we have transparent OLEDs, we have foldable O LED, we have top emitting OLED and white O LED.
[00:09:26.148] Let us look at each one of them carefully what are these different types of O LEDs which we are referring to. The first one is a passive matrix O LED, and here we have strips of these cathode.
[00:09:43.460] and anode and the organic layers. The anode strips are arranged perpendicular to the cathode strips and the intersection of the cathode and anode they form the pixels from where the light is emitted.

Transcript block 3 (source interval 000600-000899 seconds):
[00:10:00.452] There has to be an external circuitry here which applies current to selected strips of anode and cathode, thereby determining which pixel should be turned on and which pixel should be turned off.
[00:10:16.100] So because of this external circuitry here, the power consumption is more compared to the other OLEDs, and therefore these are mostly used for small screens.
[00:10:30.180] Coming to active matrix OLEDs which are more popular and many of the mobile displays now they use this amulet. Now they what do they have? They have a full layer of cathode, organic molecules, and anode.
[00:10:46.852] Here the anode layer has a thin film transistor TFT array at the back plate. There is a back plate of TFT and that forms a matrix.
[00:10:59.492] Now this TFT array itself is the circuitry and that determines which pixels get turned on to form the image.
[00:11:10.564] Now amulets therefore consume less power than the P amulets because the TFT array requires less power as compared to the external circuitry and therefore they are very efficient for large displays.
[00:11:28.356] like we have electronic uh signages or we have these big TVs, large screen TVs. Transparent OLEDs. They consist of a transparent substrate, cathode and anode.
[00:11:46.692] So when a transparent OLED display is turned on, it allows light to pass in both the directions as you can see here. And a transparent OLED display can be either active matrix type or a passive matrix type.
[00:12:01.600] And it is used in transparent projector screens and glasses. The next one is a top editing OLED. So basically you can see here it's only in one direction. So they have a substrate that is either opaque or reflective.
[00:12:20.132] They are best suited for active metrics design and they are used for making small card displays.
[00:12:28.900] Then foldable O LEDs. They have the substrate made of very flexible metal foils or plastics, as you can see here, and they are very lightweight, ultra thin and
[00:12:42.032] and because they are foldable they can reduce the breakage of displays. So we understand they can be used in cell phones and PDAs. Personal digital assistance.
[00:12:56.676] Now coming to the last one that is white OLED. Now these emit white light that is brighter, more uniform, and more energy efficient than that emitted by fluorescent lights.
[00:13:10.340] They give you true color quality like of incandescent lighting, and therefore they can be used for large and efficient lighting systems. Let us see what are the advantages of OLEDs.
[00:13:26.372] The organic lay of an OLED are thinner, lighter, and more flexible than the crystalline layers of LED or L CD. We know that in the market we have L C D or
[00:13:40.484] TVs and then came the LED TVs. And now there's a lot of talk about O LED screens.
[00:13:49.604] They are brighter than LEDs because the organic layer of an O LED are much thinner than the corresponding inorganic crystal layers which are used in LED.
[00:14:02.820] And so the conductive and the emissing emissive lay of an OLED can be multi-layered. So you get a very bright picture. And of course they consume much less power than the L C D's.
[00:14:18.820] and then easier to produce and can be made in large sizes and they have large fields of view.
[00:14:27.172] In an L C D we know that if we go at an angle we will not be able to see the picture. That is not the case with O L E D. Up to 170 degrees the viewing angle has now become very large and there's a very high color contrast and faster response time.
[00:14:48.324] So what are the disadvantages? They have shorter lifespan and the manufacturing process is expensive. And one of the most important problem we face with OLEDs is water can easily damage them.

Transcript block 4 (source interval 000900-001199 seconds):
[00:15:08.004] What are the applications? They are used in mobile phone displays. And then we have digital cameras where they can be used. And lighting. As we said, white bullets, they can be used for lighting.
[00:15:24.836] Then we have audio video players and then we have OLED TVs and then also different
[00:15:36.900] Other type of devices like wristwatches, so displays in wristwatches, etc. And if they are foldable, you can put it right over your wrist. So these are the applications of OLEPs.
[00:15:51.492] So that brings us to the end of module seven A. And in the next class we will be talking about green chemistry, which is the last class of unit five. Thank you.
